summary: Defines MIB objects for managing Ethernet-like interfaces. It is historic. It was replaced by RFC 3638.

eli5.summary: Gauges for checking Ethernet network cards. A newer list replaced it.

questions: what statistics does ethernet management track
how is ethernet monitored with snmp
subtitle: Measuring Ethernet performance with SNMP network management objects.

tldr.problem: Network administrators need a standard way to collect statistics and error counters from Ethernet interfaces using network management protocols.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1643 defines a set of Management Information Base (MIB) objects that expose Ethernet statistics like collision rates, frame errors, and transmission metrics through SNMP.
tldr.outcome: Network management systems could query these standardized counters to monitor Ethernet interface health. This RFC is now Historic and has been replaced by RFC 3638.

today: RFC 1643 is Historic, superseded by RFC 3638. It obsoletes RFC 1623 and corrects errors from RFC 1398. While new implementations should use RFC 3638, the objects defined here remain documented for backward compatibility with existing systems.

sections.title: Introduction to Ethernet Management
sections.content:
RFC 1643 defines a set of management objects for monitoring Ethernet-like network interfaces. These objects fit into the Management Information Base (MIB), a standardized way of exposing information about network devices through SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol).

The RFC focuses on three types of Ethernet interfaces identified in the Internet-standard MIB: ethernet-csmacd, iso88023-csmacd, and starLan. For these interfaces, the RFC provides a common set of statistics and error counters that SNMP management systems can query to assess interface health and performance.
sections.eli5: Imagine your Ethernet card reports how many packets were sent, how many collisions happened, and what kinds of errors occurred. This RFC is the rulebook for what numbers to report and how to organize them.

sections.title: SNMP and the Management Framework
sections.content:
The RFC operates within the SNMP Network Management Framework, which has three main components. First, the Structure of Management Information (SMI) defines how to describe and name managed objects. Second, the Management Information Base (MIB) is a collection of managed objects for the Internet suite of protocols. Third, SNMP itself is the protocol that allows management stations to access and manipulate these objects on managed devices.

Managed objects are accessed through a virtual information store called the MIB. Objects in the MIB are defined using a subset of Abstract Syntax Notation One (ASN.1) and are identified by an OBJECT IDENTIFIER, an administratively assigned hierarchical name.
sections.eli5: SNMP is like a language that lets a management computer ask network devices questions. This RFC defines what questions you can ask about Ethernet cards and what answers you should expect.

sections.title: Ethernet Statistics Objects
sections.content:
The main statistics group (dot3StatsTable) contains counters for a collection of Ethernet-like interfaces. Each interface has a row in the table with counters for various types of errors and transmission events. The counters include alignment errors (frames that are not a whole number of octets), FCS errors (frames that fail the Frame Check Sequence), collision statistics, and transmission errors.

The RFC also defines carrier sense errors (when the medium appears busy), deferred transmissions (when sending is delayed because the medium is busy), and frame-too-long errors (oversized frames). Each interface also reports an EtherChipset identifier, which allows a management station to correlate statistics with the specific hardware chip generating them and account for any known chip anomalies.
sections.eli5: Think of the statistics group as a dashboard showing counts: how many packets got lost, how many times two devices tried to send at once (collision), and how many times the wire was too busy. Each Ethernet card has one dashboard.

sections.title: Collision Analysis and Interface Testing
sections.content:
The RFC defines a collision histogram (dot3CollTable) that records how many frames experienced exactly one collision, two collisions, and so on, up to sixteen collisions. This helps network operators understand the load and congestion on an Ethernet segment.

The RFC also specifies two tests that can be invoked on Ethernet interfaces. The TDR test (Time-Domain Reflectometry) measures the time from the start of transmission until a collision is detected or the carrier signal drops, helping identify cable faults. The Loopback test configures the MAC chip to test its own memory, data paths, and logic internally. Both tests are optional; many interface chips do not support them.
sections.eli5: Sometimes Ethernet cards can run self-tests, like a computer checking its own memory. The collision histogram is like a graph showing when the network was congested.
